claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has superior plastic strain relative to pure tungsten under high-temperature loading.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has superior toughness relative to pure tungsten under high-temperature loading.
The WTaTiVZr alloy contains inherent atomic-scale lattice distortions that generate heterogeneous local stress fields.
Lattice distortions in WTaTiVZr promote enhanced dynamic recovery.
Lattice distortions in WTaTiVZr lower barriers to dislocation motion.
Lattice distortions activate additional deformation modes, including cross-slip and possibly twinning.
Enhanced recovery and additional dislocation modes delay dislocation pile-up.
The proposed deformation mechanisms produce a refined, heterogeneous deformation substructure.
The refined substructure delays crack initiation.
Delayed crack initiation and heterogeneous deformation improve ductility and toughness.
The starting WTaTiVZr material can be prepared as a homogeneous, single-phase alloy.
Under matched high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will begin plastic deformation earlier than pure tungsten.
Under matched high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater plastic strain to failure than pure tungsten.
Under matched high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will absorb more energy before fracture than pure tungsten.
TEM and EBSD will show more dynamic recovery, subgrain refinement, and heterogeneous dislocation activity in WTaTiVZr than in pure tungsten.
Commercially used pure tungsten has limited plasticity and toughness under the stated loading conditions.
Pure tungsten's limited plasticity and toughness are caused by its comparatively uniform lattice structure.
Temperatures above approximately 1000 degrees Celsius are relevant to sustained plasma-facing-component mechanical service.
The proposed lattice-distortion mechanism may not be significant at lower temperatures.
Matching grain size, atmosphere, strain rate, and initial microstructure is intended to isolate intrinsic alloy-dependent behavior.
